newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEKS ALLOWED FOREX DEPOSITS, CONTROLS LIFTED.
newsitem.headline: GREEKS ALLOWED FOREX DEPOSITS, CONTROLS LIFTED.

text.p: The Bank of Greece moved to lift remaining foreign exchange controls allowing Greek residents and legal entities to hold foreign exchange deposits with local credit institutions effective August 1.

"Greek residents, individuals and legal entities, will be allowed to hold deposits in foreign currency without limitations with credit institutions operating in Greece effective August 1 1997," the central bank said.
It was the remaining chapter in fully liberalising Greece's foreign exchange market.
In May 1994, the central bank had allowed Greek residents to hold foreign currency assets and deposits with credit institutions abroad.
Starting August 1, under decree 2416, forex deposits may be opened with foreign currency banknotes obtained abroad or purchased against drachmas in Greece.
To open these accounts and maintain them Greeks will no longer face any red tape as to the origin of the foreign money. Only regulations related to law 2331 on money laundering will still apply.
Depositors will henceforth be allowed to make withdrawals in foreign currency or drachmas from these accounts and to transfer funds or make payments abroad, the central bank said.
Maturities, interest rates and other terms on these foreign currency deposits will be the outcome of a free market.
Also, the existing classes of forex deposits by Greek residents -- sailors and repatriated immigrants -- will gradually cease to be subject to a mandatory 70 percent redeposit with the central bank.
The regime will be aligned with the required reserve ratio of 12 percent currently in force as regards drachma deposits.
Moreover, the 0.4 percent interest-rate premium on foreign currency deposits that pay interest in drachmas will be phased out, the Bank of Greece said.
And based on decree 2417, Greeks will no longer be obliged to convert to drachmas assets they repatriate. As of August 1, repatriated assets may be held in foreign currency.
The Bank of Greece also removed the 20,000 ecu limit which applied to personal cheques and cash when traveling abroad or making cross-border payments without the intermediation of banks.

Foreign currency deposits held by individuals and legal entities domiciled in Greece are subject to a 15 percent witholding tax on earned interest since January 1 1997 as is the case for drachma deposits.
